newsitem.title: POLAND: POLISH NBP RATE RISE SEEN SYMBOLIC, IF AT ALL - MKT.
newsitem.headline: POLISH NBP RATE RISE SEEN SYMBOLIC, IF AT ALL - MKT.

text.p: The National Bank of Poland may not have to go through with it warning of an official rate rise in January because market rates have already jumped more than 2.5 points over the last four weeks, analysts said.

They said that even if the central bank decided to raise its official rates, now at 22 and 25 percent, the move would not be more than one point and would, to a large extent, be ignored by traders, who watch market rates.

"Despite lots of talk, the NBP is unlikely to touch nominal rates. But if it does, the rise may not even be one point, only to signal the direction," said Wlodzimierz Osak, chief dealer at Pekao SA bank.
"The market's reaction to such a rise would be minimal because it has already been priced in current market rates," Osak said.
Analysts said December broad money and inflation data, likely to be released next week, could give the market some indication of whether the NBP was planning to raise rates.

Since December the central bank has been signaling that it might be forced to raise its discount and lombard rates early this year if credit for households, which doubled in 1996 against 1995, continues to boom this year.

The NBP had also noted that 1997's larger than planned budget deficit of 2.8 percent of gross doemstic product would make the fight to cut inflation to 13 percent at the end of this year from about 18.5 percent in 1996 even more difficult.
The bank has said it wanted market and nominal rates to converge and boosted the former from around 19.5 percent to about 22.0 percent through NBP-bill sales and reverse repos.
"I don't see a need for a nominal rate rise...the NBP already raised the most important market rates," said Jacek Lech deputy chief dealer at bank Handlowy SA.
Lech said that by raising market rates the NBP provided banks with an attractive alternative to unliquid consumer credit, in which banks have been placing cash surpluses.

Some dealers said, however, the NBP may want to increase nominal rates more as a signal to consumers than to banks to discourage them from taking more credit, and to slow down inflationary money supply growth.
They also said an official rate rise of about one percent would narrow the current gap between the average yields of T-bills and NBP-bills of the same maturity.

At the last primary auction the 26-week paper sold at an average yield of 19.37 percent while a 182-day NBP-bill sold at 22.0 percent. A 13-week T-bill yield was last at 18.99 percent while a 91-day NBP paper gave 21.99 percent.
"I would expect a one point rate rise because there has to be some correlation between nominal and market rates," said Krzysztof Kozuchowski, T-bill dealer at ING bank in Warsaw.
"Such a rise would boost T-bill yields and narrow the spread against NBP-bills from the current ludicrous 250 basis points to a more acceptable 150 basis points," he said.
